# build-loop

**After compaction: reread this skill.** A summary keeps the task but loses
these rules. When a session that used build-loop comes back from compaction,
reread this file, `vigil` and the reference for the step you are on before any other step. If work is in
flight, re-arm a vigil hold and start its background keepalive in that turn (§10). Compaction summaries preserve the reread and live-hold requirement.

This file is a router; detail lives in `references/`. Section numbers are stable.

**Load the companions.**

| Skill | Load it when |
|---|---|
| `technical-excellence` | Before design or code, and when judging a finding. |
| `test-quality` | Before red, when tests come back, when a fix touches a test. |
| `question-everything` | Before a spec and before green (§4a). |
| `vigil` | As soon as work is in flight (§10); `manual-keepalive` only if vigil fails. |
| `qex`, `low-ram-hosts` | Before any heavy job (§8–9). |

**Load the references at their step.**

| File | Read it |
|---|---|
| `references/phases.md` | Before §3, before launching red, before green. |
| `references/roles.md`, `references/dialogue.md` | Before every implementer or reviewer brief; roles also on budget advice or reset. |
| `references/review.md`, `-v2.md` | Before review round 1 (§6: bar, rounds, checkpoint, answering, ledger, v2 schedule). |
| `references/bars.md` | At `review-ledger init`, to choose the bar (§6a). |
| `references/bots.md` | When a PR bot posts (§6e). |
| `references/sol.md` | Before the first Sol run (§7). |
| `references/scoping.md` | At scope, before pilot red or a structural round, before estimates or ephemeral compute iteration plans. |
| `references/budget.md` | On budget advice, a usage limit or reset, before a second agent, on a vigil `item overdue` (§8–§10). |
| `references/reviewers.md` | Before a contribution to a project you do not own, before re-scoping a PR after review. |
| `references/handoff.md` | Before a PR body or the final report (§11–§12). |

Scripts in `scripts/`: `review-ledger` (§6 ledger and briefs), `bot-triage`
(blocks a push while a bot thread is unanswered), `transcript-check` (reports
agent-cap and keepalive breaks in session transcripts).

## Dialogue before work advances

Every agent reviewer, including spec and final reviewers and clean approvals,
needs at least one substantive argument exchange with the orchestrator per round.
Fable needs at least two; keep the existing two-exchange rule on non-clean round 4.
Challenge an assumption or explain why a simpler design suffices; do not invent
disagreement. Implementers start work immediately. Roughly five minutes in,
the orchestrator reads 1–5 relevant files, asks about ambiguities and 2–3
work-grounded questions, hears the answers, then pushes back and settles the
direction. Short batches get this check at handoff. Details: `dialogue.md`.

Every brief states most-important behavior, invariants, priority concerns, lower
priorities and evidence. Preserve serious defects regardless of priority. Use
`references/dialogue.md` and the ledger to record focus and dialogue. No upfront
proposal approval.

## 0. Boldness

Put this in your stance and every implementer prompt:

> Remember that you are motherfucking powerful. You need to go full gas, balls to the wall. Get this crazy shit done. Be ambitious. Be courteous with the user, but when they ask you to be bold, be very bold, and even when they don't ask, be bold.

Bold means big, well-aimed batches and firm pushback on weak findings, never
skipping verification, scope control or approval gates. Boldness never raises
the agent cap (§2): bold means a bigger, better-aimed single run.

**Stance (owner 2026-11-13).** If you think this is a good idea, do it.
Otherwise, suggest something else. Tell the owner when they are about to do
something dumb. On judgement calls (scope, design, worth fixing) weigh Fable's
unusual claims more than Sol's; a test settles facts, not either model.

## 1. Feature discussion (before any engineering)

Do this first, in order:

0. **Scope.** Ask: a pilot (a few cases, gather data, then decide), a
   structural fix, or hardening? Default: pilot; ask inline and
   keep working (§1a). A pilot gets its own branch and stays a reference; the
   structural round starts fresh. Pilot rules: `references/scoping.md`. Until hardening,
   test the design, not the symptom; every implementer brief carries the 30-minute flag and "never vigil orchestrator mode".
1. **Simpler alternative.** Does a simpler way exist (do less, reuse, change
   the requirement)?
2. **Desires.** Their first-order desire (what they asked for), second-order
   desire (why), and threat model (who can reach it, untrusted inputs, what it holds).
3. **Debate Socratically.** Question assumptions and offer counter-cases and
   cheaper options. Then write the agreed intent in 1-2 sentences: the review
   brief's Intent.

Skip only for a fix whose intent is already unambiguous. If the user may be
away, take the sensible default and log it (§1a). Poorly scoped work: ask for
more detail first (`question-everything`).

## 1a. Owner contact and decisions

Assume the user is away: ask inline with a default and keep working.
AskUserQuestion only on request: it blocks. Never block; take the safe default and log it as "Defaults taken" (`references/roles.md`).

## 2. Roles and budget

**Agent cap.** One working Claude agent (Opus, Sonnet, Fable, Haiku) at a time.
Reviewers have a separate cap of one. Only the owner raises the cap; log the
raise with an end condition (a time or a task), and when it ends, count again
before every launch. Implementers, authors, researchers, integrators, spec
writers and investigators all count, and changing model or role never changes
the cap. "Economical" means usage first, wall-clock second, so parallel authors
are never economical. If one owner message holds several requests, state an
order and run them one after another. This cap outranks the harness's general
advice to parallelise. Before every `delegate_task` or Agent call, check in one
line: working Claude agents now (`vigil status <hold>` lists the items; count the Claude-run ones; Codex/Sol
runs and commands do not count, reviewers count against their own cap) are under the cap, and the
run serves the owner's priority workstream, else queue it. Codex and Sol runs
are less strict: run them in parallel when it helps, but watch their limits,
which run out faster now.

| Role | Default | Does |
|---|---|---|
| Orchestrator | Opus (you) | Specs, prompts, verification, commits, pushes, owner contact. Writes little code. |
| Implementer | Sonnet and Sol, alternating by fix round (B1) | Red tests, green code, fixes. |
| Reviewer, rounds 1-2 | Sol or Opus | Scored fix rounds (§6). Reviews only, plus comment fixups. |
| Reviewer, round 3 | Fable 5.2 or later | The "good enough to ship" call (§6). |
| Reviewer, tier 2 | Fresh Opus (Fable if Opus wrote code) | One pass on the stable diff. |

B1–B5, R2 (a reviewer never reviews code it wrote), C3, budget switching and
batching: `references/roles.md`. Never quietly substitute a model for a role
the user pinned. State who holds which role at the start of each phase.

## 3–5. Scope, red, spec gate, green

Find the base, ONE diff command (§3). One red run for the whole scope; verify
the red gate yourself, commit red (§4). Spec gate before green (§4a). Green in
batches, verified and committed per phase (§5). Shared tree: `git commit
--only -- <paths>`; never stash. Steps: `references/phases.md`.

## 6. Review loop (scored, bounded)

After green, or before filing a PR, review runs across model families, then
bots get triaged (§6e). **Read `references/review.md` and
`references/review-v2.md` before round 1**; drive the rounds with
`scripts/review-ledger`.

Stages: pilot → structural → hardening. Pilots use agreed bars, round-2 Fable and owner approval; see `scoping.md`. Integration branches the owner runs need structural review; upstream PRs and project releases need hardening.

Rounds 1–2 use Sol or Opus, excluding authors. Round 3 uses Fable, then a
step-back if needed. Rounds 4–5 follow the documented pivot schedule; stop
stuck after five. Each round completes its argument minimum before advancing.
The pilot schedule, score bars, checkpoint, cull and final-fix rules remain in
`references/review-v2.md`.

Tier 2 is a fresh Opus pass, or Fable if Opus wrote code. After a passing
Fable round there is no tier 2. A ledger without `schema: 2` keeps the legacy
schedule. Run Sol per §7; run Opus as a subagent (`model: opus`) with the
review-only brief and no history. In `references/`: **6a** replies carry
`SCORE[concern]: n/10` against bars; only `needed for bar: yes` blocks; **6b** full diff in round 1, then diff-only
(a timeout is not approval); **6c** which layer stops each bug class; **6d**
smallest fix, failing test first, never agree to end the loop; **6e** PR bots,
`bot-triage guard` before each push; **A7** comment fixups only.

## 7. Running Sol

T3 `delegate_task` first, then `codex`; no Sol route: report the blocker,
substitute no model. `references/sol.md`.

## 8–9. Usage limits and concurrency

On a usage limit: save partial work, wait for the reset, probe, resume; never
restart. The cap is §2. Heavy work runs on ephemeral compute, the few local
jobs through qex. Extra implementers get their own worktree; forbid `git
stash`. `references/budget.md`, `references/scoping.md`.

## 10. Keepalive and low-budget conduct

**Hold the session with vigil** while anything is in flight, even with nothing
to watch: each wait also checks usage limits and advisories. Manual tick only
if vigil is unavailable or failing; never loops or chained sleeps.

**Wait in the background:** `vigil keepalive <hold> --orchestrator`,
`run_in_background`, timeout at least 3,600,000 ms; on each return, act and
start the next. Subagents never use orchestrator mode. One session hold
(bare is fine); each delegated run is an item: `vigil hold add <hold> --for
pid:N|file:<report>|none --expect-s N --label <run>`, and `vigil hold done
<hold> <run>` on a `none` run's notification. Never cancel it; if it
releases, make a new hold in the same turn.

"In flight": a working or paused subagent, Sol run or reviewer; a background
command; a wait on CI, a bot or a usage reset; queued work; or the user asked
(only they end it). Never end a turn with work in flight and no live hold.

Long jobs and low budget: `references/budget.md` §10.

## 11. Ship

Push only if the user asked to push, ship or update the PR; never during the
loop. Outward actions (PRs, comments, upstream pushes) need approval; show the
draft first. PR body line: `references/handoff.md`.

## 12. Hand-off report

Contents: `references/handoff.md`.

# question-everything

A defect costs least in a sentence of the spec, more in a red test, and most
in reviewed code. Spend questions early.

| Skill | Load it when |
|---|---|
| `build-loop` | The feature is multi-phase; this skill is its pre-green gate (build-loop §4a). |
| `technical-excellence` | Shaping interfaces, invariants and types while you question the spec. |
| `test-quality` | Judging whether the red tests prove the spec. |

## 1. Interview the designer

The user is the designer. Get high-fidelity detail before anyone writes code.
Push back: an answer that leaves a state, edge or failure undefined is not an
answer yet.

Ask, with a proposed default for each, so the user can answer in a word:
1. **States.** Every state the thing can be in, including empty, unknown,
   partial, stale, refused, failed. What does the user see in each?
2. **Edges.** Time (midnight, time zones, DST, nights that cross dates),
   units, limits, duplicates, retries, concurrency, offline, first run,
   upgrade from old data.
3. **Lifecycle of data.** Created, edited, deleted, exported, restored,
   merged, migrated: what happens to this feature's data on each path?
4. **Precedence.** When two sources disagree (user edit vs derived value,
   local vs backup, old vs new), which wins, and is that visible?
5. **Safety.** What must never happen (e.g. "never tell a wearer to skip a
   prescribed drug")? Write it as an invariant the types or tests enforce.
6. **Look.** Layout constraints the user cares about (stable row height,
   locked visuals). Get a mockup or golden description.
7. **Checklists.** "Which checklists should this run through?" Offer the
   project's existing ones as defaults (see §3).
8. **Reuse.** "What here could be reused elsewhere, or should reuse
   something that exists?" Offer your own candidates first.

If the user is away, take the safe default, log it, and raise it later
(build-loop §1a). Never block.

## 2. Ask yourself the same questions

Before writing the spec, answer §1 yourself from the code:
- grep for existing seams that already solve part of it (a reconcile helper,
  a write seam, a scheduler, an id generator), and require their use;
- list every path the data travels (§1.3) and name the code for each;
- list the invariants and how each is enforced (type > test > review);
- list what is unknown, and how unknown stays unknown (never a silent zero).

## 3. Turn recurrence into checklists, early

Watch review findings across features. When the same family shows up twice
(e.g. "new table missing from export/restore", "delta arithmetic drifts from
the canonical total"), stop and write or extend a project checklist. Do not
wait for a fifth round. Keep checklists in the project (not in a generic
skill), each item citing the findings that taught it. Every later spec that
touches that area pastes the checklist, and the implementer answers each line
("done: <test>" or "n/a: <reason>").

Also ask at each feature start: "Which recurring families could this
feature hit?" and pre-empt them in the spec.

## 4. Cross-model spec review (before green)

After the red phase commits and before any green code:
1. Send the reviewer (e.g. Sol) the spec, the red tests, the applicable
   checklists, and the designer's answers. Ask for: gaps (states, edges,
   lifecycle paths, precedence), contradictions, tests that would pass
   without the feature, missing invariants, and simpler designs or reuse.
2. Exchange at least one substantive argument with each spec reviewer before
   accepting its review, even an approval. Fable needs at least two. Give the
   reviewer the round priorities and invariants; record the exchange using
   build-loop `references/dialogue.md`. Fix the spec and red tests, then rerun the red gate.
3. At most two spec rounds. Anything still open after round two becomes an
   explicit decision (default + log + raise), not a third round.
4. Then implement, and run the normal code review loop (build-loop §6).

The spec review is cheap: no code to read, so it should take one run.
Findings here save whole code-review rounds later.

## 5. Signs you skipped this

- review rounds keep finding new cases of the same family;
- fixes introduce ids, flags or columns the spec never mentioned;
- the implementer picks between designs mid-green ("I chose X over Y");
- defaults are discovered in reports instead of decided in the spec.

When you see these, pause the loop and come back here.

# technical-excellence

Standards for what the code says and how it is shaped.

| Skill | Load it when |
|---|---|
| `test-quality` | Writing or reviewing the tests that prove an interface, claim or invariant here. |
| `build-loop` | The work is multi-phase, or a cross-model review will judge it. Its review step uses sections 6 and 7 below. |

First rule: **when in Rome.** Follow the repo's conventions (AGENTS.md,
existing style, lexicon) before anything below. Apply this skill where the repo
is silent.

## 1. Rich interfaces

An interface is more than signatures. Each abstraction documents:

| Part | Says |
|---|---|
| Error detail | What can fail, and how it is reported (type, code, null, exception). Callers must be able to handle each case without reading the body. |
| Reason | Why it exists. What breaks or duplicates if it is removed. |
| Invariants | What is always true before, during and after calls. |
| Mating parts | If it has a second or third counterpart (writer/reader, encoder/decoder, client/server), name them. |

**Mated parts need parity tests** proving both sides agree: round trip, plus
independent fixtures (see `test-quality`, parity and oracles). A pair that is
only tested against each other's constants proves nothing.

## 2. Claims are cited

Module-level comments and comments above code blocks contain verifiable
claims ("this is O(n)", "the device sends big-endian", "idempotent",
"commit happens before ACK"). Every such claim is anchored and sourced.

Convention (adapt the comment syntax to the language):

```
// CLAIM(ack-order): the commit completes before the ACK is sent [spec §4.2; ack_order_test]
...
// ↳ CLAIM(ack-order)
ack(token);
```

- The comment states a **verifiable** claim and its **source or proof** in
  brackets: a spec section, capture file, proof sketch, or test name.
- The code the claim governs carries `↳ CLAIM(<id>)`.
- A maintainer changing that code greps the id, finds the claim and its
  proof, and re-checks it.
- Tests that prove the claim name the id in their why (`test-quality`).
- Ids are short, unique, stable. Unprovable "claims" are opinions: label them
  as such or delete them. A comment with no source is a rumor.

## 3. Deep modules

Prefer a simple interface over a substantial implementation. Few entry
points, few parameters, no leaked internals. Smells: shallow wrappers that
forward one call; interfaces as long as the body; callers that must know
call order. Hide the complexity; do not spread it across callers.

## 4. Lexicon and naming

Keep a project lexicon (a glossary doc: term, meaning, where it lives). Name
code in correspondence with it. Add a term to the glossary when you coin one;
do not use two words for one concept.

Outside any convention:

- Clear names, **no abbreviations**.
- 1-2 primary words, plus optional small words (determiners, prepositions):
  `rowsToPrune`, `nightOfRecord`.
- Be deliberate about grammar:
  - functions and methods: verbs (`parseFrame`); predicates read as
    questions (`isFinalized`, `hasPendingWrite`);
  - values and types: nouns (`dayLabel`, `HistoryToken`);
  - qualifiers: adjectives (`pendingRows`);
  - tense shows state: `committedRows` (done), `rowsToCommit` (not yet).
- Name by how the value is used, not its type. Avoid vague names such as
  `value`, `data`, `result`, `tmp`. A function that sums two numbers returns
  `sum`; a truly generic result is `returnValue`.

## 5. Type-level safety first

Algorithmic and algebraic design shrinks runtime checks, tests and review.
Reach for these before adding a check:

| Tool | Effect |
|---|---|
| Make invalid states unrepresentable (sum types, non-empty lists, state enums carrying only valid fields) | The bug cannot compile. No test or review needed. |
| Newtypes / branded types (`LocalDayLabel` vs `UtcTimestamp`, `Milliseconds` vs `Seconds`) | Mixed-up units and ids fail to compile. |
| Exhaustive matching, no default branch | Adding a case forces every consumer to be updated. |
| Monoids (identity, associative combine) for accumulators | Split-merge equals single pass; parallelism and incrementality are safe. Prove laws with property tests (`test-quality`). |
| Parse, don't validate: convert raw input to a checked type once, at the boundary | Inner code never re-checks. |
| Smart constructors, private fields | Invariants hold by construction. |

If a runtime check or a test exists only to catch an invalid state a type
could forbid, change the type.

## 6. Security stance review

Security judgments are made against a **threat model**, never by reflex.

1. Use the project's existing framework (a residual-risk framework, AGENTS.md
   invariants, an existing model).
2. If none exists, write a short `THREAT_MODEL.md`: assets, actors, trust
   boundaries, in scope, out of scope. Leave it UNCOMMITTED unless the user
   says otherwise.
3. Question the stance itself: which assets matter most, who can reach which
   boundary, what is knowingly accepted. Record accepted risks with a reason.
4. For each security-relevant change or review comment, decide: real exposure
   under the model, hardening nicety, or out of scope. State which and why.
5. Where a project limits reviewers to correctness findings, honor that for
   what you ask of them, but still assess security yourself.

## 7. Judging review findings

A finding is not a nit because it is small. Check it against: the claim it
contradicts (section 2), the invariant it breaks (section 1), the type that
could prevent it (section 5), and the threat model (section 6). Then apply
the smallest fix, with a test that fails without it (`test-quality`).

# Test quality

A green run says nothing about whether a test can fail. For every test you
write or review, answer one question: **if the bug came back, would this go
red?** If you can't name the bug it catches, it's hollow.

| Skill | Load it when |
|---|---|
| `technical-excellence` | The test proves an interface, invariant or CLAIM, or a type could make the test unnecessary. Source of the CLAIM convention and mated-part (parity) rule. |
| `build-loop` | You are in a red/green run or a review round. Its red gate uses this skill; review findings about tests are judged with it. |

## 1. Every test says why

The reason a test exists is hard to recall later. Annotate each test with a
short WHY: the bug, rule, incident or claim it guards.

```
// why: a partial chunk must never be ACKed (invariant 3.1; regression of the
//      2026-09 early-ack bug). Fails if commit moves after ack.
// proves: CLAIM(ack-order)
```

- A test proving a CLAIM (see `technical-excellence`) names its id, so the
  claim's grep finds its proof.
- No why, no keep: a test whose purpose nobody can state is a deletion
  candidate.
- Expected values show their derivation (spec section, capture, arithmetic).

## 2. Placement

Co-locate tests with the code they test, unless the repo's convention says
otherwise (when in Rome). A test beside its module shows what the abstraction
is, travels with it, and is deleted with it. Cross-cutting and end-to-end
suites live apart, and say so in their why.

## 3. Techniques worth using

### Monoids and accumulators
If a type combines (`combine`, identity element), property-test the laws:

| Law | Property |
|---|---|
| Identity | `combine(x, empty) == x == combine(empty, x)` |
| Associativity | `combine(combine(a,b),c) == combine(a,combine(b,c))` |
| Commutativity | `combine(a,b) == combine(b,a)` (only if claimed) |
| Split-merge | for any split of the input, `combine(fold(left), fold(right)) == fold(whole)` (single pass equals chunked/parallel/incremental) |

Generate inputs randomly with a fixed seed; shrink failures.

### State machines
Model-based property tests: a small pure model of the intended states and
transitions; generate random command sequences; apply to model and real
system; assert observable state agrees after every step, and that illegal
transitions are refused. Include crash/rollback and retry commands.

### Oracles
Expected values come from something independent of the code under test:
- a slow, obviously-correct reference implementation;
- a hand-computed fixture (arithmetic in a comment);
- a real capture or spec table, decoded field by field.
Beware a shared oracle: incremental-vs-forced parity can pass while both
paths inherit the same regression. Keep an independently derived fixture next
to the parity test.

### Goldens
High quality means: reviewed by a person, minimal (smallest input that shows
the behavior), deterministic (zone, clock, seed, locale pinned), explained
(why: what it pins, version or pin it was generated at). Regeneration is a
deliberate, flagged act, never silent. A golden nobody inspected is mode 12.
Retain exact comparison for a fixed version; do not hide change behind a
blanket tolerance.

### Parity tests for mated interfaces
Writer/reader, encoder/decoder, client/server: test both against literal
bytes or messages from the spec or a real capture, field by field, not just
against each other. Round-trip tests are a supplement, never the proof.
Dedupe parity corpora and report the real unique count.

## 4. Mutation checks

**Cheap manual mutations (do these every time).** Pick 3-5 spots in the code
under test, mutate one at a time, run the focused tests:

| Mutation | If still green |
|---|---|
| Flip a condition (`<` to `<=`, `&&` to `\|\|`, negate) | Boundary or branch untested |
| Delete a line or a call | That line is unproven; or the test is at the wrong layer |
| Change a constant (offset, threshold, default) | Value not asserted exactly |
| Swap two arguments or an ordering | Order not pinned |

Use the result to decide: more tests needed, or tests that prove nothing
(remove them). Revert every mutation; never commit one.

**`# catches:` and post-green spot mutations (build-loop red/green).** Each
red test carries a `# catches: <a plausible wrong implementation this fails>`
line. If you cannot name one, the test is likely a tautology; rewrite or drop
it. After green, the orchestrator applies 2-3 of those named wrong
implementations and checks the matching tests go red. A green implementer that
edits a red test says so in its report; the edit becomes a review finding.

**Mutation tool, periodically.** If the stack has one (for example Stryker,
mutmut, cargo-mutants, PIT), run it every so often on a stable module.
Surviving mutants show gaps. Tests that kill no unique mutant and duplicate
another test's kills are candidates to prune, which keeps the standard suite
small and fast.

## 5. Hunt tautology explicitly

Before approving any test, ask of each assertion: *can this expression be
false given any implementation?* Tautology signs: value compared to itself;
mock returns what it was told; expected computed by the function under test;
a literal's length asserted on the literal; a test of a pasted copy; a
mirrored formula. Mode 1 and 5 below, with fixes. For tautology, the
tool is the "revert the fix" mutation.

## 6. The mutation check that catches most failure modes

Mentally (or actually) mutate the code under test and see if the test fails:

1. Revert the fix the test claims to pin. Still green? The test is wrong.
2. Delete the call site the test claims to cover (not the helper: the place
   production calls it). Still green? Wrong layer.
3. Empty the list, set or config the test iterates over. Still green? Vacuous.
4. Run it under `TZ=UTC` and under a DST zone. Different result, or a skip?
   Host-dependent.
5. Remove the fixture file. Skip with no CI failure? It never runs in CI.

bug.

## 7. Classic modes

| # | Mode | Looks like | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Tautology | Value compared to itself; mock returns what it was told; expected computed by the function under test; `hasLength(12)` on a 12-item literal; `isNotNull` on a tear-off | Expected value from the spec or a hand calculation |
| 2 | Over-mocking | The engine/unit under test is stubbed; only fakes run | Mock the clock, network, platform. Never the unit |
| 3 | Asserts current behavior | Magic numbers with no derivation (`9.03`, `closeTo(50, 8)`); comment-free goldens | Show the arithmetic in a comment, or cite the spec/capture the value came from |
| 4 | Happy path only | No empty, null, zero, negative, NaN, boundary, duplicate, truncated, error, or thin-input case | List the edge cases before writing the first test |
| 5 | Mirrored implementation | Test re-implements the formula, or tests a pasted copy of a private helper | Hand-computed constants; test the real symbol |
| 6 | Coverage theater | Code runs, nothing meaningful is asserted; benchmark tests with no `expect` | Every test asserts a concrete value |
| 7 | Existence only | `isNotNull`, `isNotEmpty`, `returnsNormally`, `greaterThan(0)`, `isA<T>()`, `verify(called)` where the exact value is known | Assert the value. If the seeded row count is 3, assert 3 |
| 8 | Weakened during a fix | Exact value became a range; case deleted; `skip:` added; tolerance widened | Treat any loosened test in a fix diff as a red flag. Change the code, not the test. `git log -p` the test file |
| 9 | Volume over quality | Dozens of near-identical cases; parity corpora where the same records repeat (978 unique of 2,934) | Fewer, distinct cases; dedupe corpora and report the real count |
| 10 | Confidently wrong | Expected value contradicts the spec, docs, or the test's own earlier assertion | Flag uncertain inputs instead of guessing |
| 11 | Unreadable failure | `expect(cond, isTrue)` with no `reason:`; byte lists without hex | Match on the value, or add `reason:` naming expected vs actual |
| 12 | Blind golden | Snapshot regenerated by an env var; nobody inspected it | Golden only reviewed output; note who checked it and against what |

## 8. Modes the classic list misses

These came up across three repos, often in tests that looked careful.

**Host-timezone dependence.** DST and local-vs-UTC tests that only bite when
the machine's zone differs from UTC, or that `markTestSkipped` unless
`TZ == America/Denver`. CI runners are UTC, so the check is vacuous there.
Calls that default to the host zone (no offset argument) also flip results
by zone. Fix: pin the zone inside the test, or pass the offset explicitly.
Never derive the expected value with the same `toLocal()` the code uses.
Run CI as a matrix: UTC plus one DST zone.

**Silently skipped fixtures.** The test skips when a data file is absent,
and that file is gitignored or lives outside the repo. CI never runs it, yet
it's often the only end-to-end or real-capture test. Fix: commit a small
fixture, or make the skip loud in CI (fail when `CI` is set). Same for sibling
checkouts: a guard that skips unless `../analytics` exists, when the real
directory is `../openstrap-analytics`, has never run anywhere. Golden groups
that skip because the golden directory is absent are the same mode.

**Source-grep guards.** "Ordering is untouched" checks that two identifiers
appear in a file; "prune order" checks `indexOf` positions; a "no 86400 s"
guard covers 22 hand-listed files and misses `86_400`. These pass if a comment
contains the string, if the code is reordered in a way the regex can't see,
or if the bug lands in an unlisted file. Fix: drive the behavior (seed a
partial day, prune, assert rows survive). Keep grep guards only as a backstop,
cover the whole tree, and include a positive control proving the pattern
matches something. A whole-tree scan for a new caller or forbidden dependency
is the legitimate kind (an audit of 88 guard files kept 18 of this type,
converted 48 to behavior tests, and removed 22).

**Pins dead code or the wrong layer.** The test exercises a pure helper, but
production reads the value through a different path. Real examples: a
readiness-flash test pinning a getter with zero callers; a freeze test that
covers the pure function but not where the screen reads or the engine writes;
a race test that never imports the service and tests `List.remove`; an "edge
half" test that only calls the sibling library; "the stager only runs inside
`Isolate.run`" checked by two strings anywhere in the file (output parity is
not execution placement). Fix: test through the seam the user hits, or add a
test that the production path calls the helper.

**Shared-table round trip.** The test builds a frame at offset 13 and the
parser reads offset 13 from the same constant. A wrong offset passes. Fix:
literal bytes from a real capture or the spec, decoded field by field. When a
real capture exists, assert every field you can hand-decode, not just the
version byte or the first 4 of 8 token bytes.

**Capability tested once, wired N times.** The new decoder is tested
directly, but two other entry points still call the old one. Fix: count the
entry points and test each, or add a guard that they all route through one.

**Iterating over the current set.** `for (op in dangerousCmds) expect(...)`
stays green when the set is emptied or an item is dropped. Fix: pin the
required members by name, then loop.

**Conditional assertions.** `if (row != null) expect(...)` passes with nothing
checked. Fix: assert the precondition first.

**Assertions on absence with no positive control.** "Nothing was written"
checked via `total_changes` or a log line, without proving the probe moves on
a real write. A no-bounce check that matches log wording passes if the log is
reworded. Fix: show the probe detects the positive case in the same test.

**Test-only configuration.** The test runs with thresholds (300/200/200) that
differ from shipped defaults (200/150/750). Fix: test the shipped defaults,
plus overrides as separate cases.

**Change-detector literals.** `expect(kAlgoVersion, 104)` or a literal SHA.
It fails on every bump and catches nothing. Fix: assert the property you care
about (the pinned commit contains the cited change).

**Real time.** `DateTime.now()`, real `Future.delayed` sleeps, and "nothing
yet" checked after 300 ms. Flaky near midnight and on slow runners; a real
one-minute wait inside a correctness test costs a minute on every run. Fix:
`fakeAsync` with `withClock`, or inject the clock.

**Tolerance that spans the plausible universe.** VO2max accepted in 30-70
when the hand value is 49.14; RMSSD up to 500 ms; one-sided bounds with no
upper limit; `closeTo(50, 8)` where the formula gives exactly 50 at z=0, so
weights and signs go untested. Fix: tolerance sized to numeric error, not to
"looks reasonable."

## 9. Domain checks worth adding wherever they apply

- **Absent input.** Missing or thin input returns null, absent, or "—", never
  a default or a value derived from another metric.
- **Idempotence.** Run the computation three times with slightly more data;
  the persisted value stays stable. Append a duplicate day; the baseline
  doesn't move.
- **Failure paths.** Every flag set on the happy path is cleared on error,
  timeout, and give-up.
- **Durability ordering.** Commit before acknowledge, tested by driving the
  real engine and observing the order, including a rollback case.
- **Ambient state.** Globals that change output are re-armed inside isolate
  closures, and a test shows output changes when they're set.

## 10. Grounding from suite audits

Two audits of a large suite (about 14,000 test blocks across three repos)
produced these lessons; use them to prioritize.

| Lesson | What to do |
|---|---|
| Many tests never ran: TZ-gated, fixture-gated, sibling-checkout-gated skips | Fix execution first (TZ matrix, committed fixtures, fail-on-skip under `CI`) before writing new tests. |
| Invariant gaps sat next to thousands of passing tests (ACK ordering, prune safety, RAM-only streams, dangerous-opcode lists) | Map each written invariant to a behavioral test that drives the real engine; grep-guards do not count. |
| Source-grep guards: 88 audited, about a fifth worth keeping | Keep whole-tree dependency/caller bans with a positive control; convert ordering/token greps to behavior; delete comment-proximity checks. |
| Shared-oracle limit: incremental-vs-forced parity passes when both inherit a regression | Keep an independent versioned fixture beside parity tests; store the generating algorithm version/pin with each golden. |
| Characterization suites overlap controller tests, but not fully | Trim case by case; do not delete wholesale. Check what the higher layer still uniquely covers (real claims, persistence, races). |
| Real waits dominated cost (a 60 s breathing session, fixed 5 s reply windows) | Inject clocks and parameterize windows; keep timing out of correctness tests. |
| Vacuous tolerances and `greaterThan(0)` everywhere | Sweep mechanically after reworks, not before, to avoid collisions. |
| A test endorsed behavior a written invariant forbids | When a test and an invariant conflict, stop and ask the owner. Do not "fix" either silently. |
| Golden baseline failed after an algorithm version bump; nothing recorded which version made it | Diff old vs new at field level; rebaseline only if all changes are the intended ones; store version and pin beside the golden. |

## 11. When writing tests (especially as a subagent)

- Write expectations from the spec before reading the implementation's
  output. Show the arithmetic.
- State each test's why and CLAIM id (section 1).
- List inputs you're unsure about instead of inventing expected values.
- Confirm each new test fails against the broken code (red first).
- Never loosen an existing assertion to make a fix pass. If it must change,
  say why in the commit message.

## 12. When reviewing

Read assertions before the green checkmark. For each test, name the bug it
catches and run the mutation check above. Report hollow tests with the
assertion quoted, the mode, and a concrete fix.

# Portable settings and one-time ADB recovery pilot

Intent: recover all configuration from the owner's prior debuggable Farhan installation without changing or uninstalling it, then provide normal file-based settings export/import that survives app signing-key changes. Notification and usage history are explicitly excluded. Base: c36faf1. Pilot branch: pilot/settings-portability; prior notification pilot remains on rework.

## Scope and storage

Source is user-authorized ADB access to a debuggable package. Wireless pairing grants shell, not root; `run-as` must succeed before export. A separate rescue APK must coexist with old and new Farhan. Package and user are explicit, default personal user 0; never assume a work-profile installation. Default package ly.com.tahaben.farhan_alpha, editable validated Android package name. No arbitrary command UI, uninstall, clear-data, package replacement, or source-file writes.

Settings span shared_prefs/shared_pref.xml, files/datastore/farhan_data_store.preferences_pb, and configuration rows in Room (apps_db and TimeLimitEntity; confirm any older DB names). Preferences cover notification app/channel/category overrides, priority locks, schedule/budgets/delivery cadence, queue preferences, exceptions, launcher/time limits/delayed launch, grayscale, scroll blocker, theme, main switches and other user configuration. Launcher activity rows include package/activity/user-serial; only restore to the same device/user initially, warn on unmatched activities. Notification/usage/launch-attempt/day-update tables are not settings. No live notification PendingIntents, runtime proxies, permission grants or Keystore keys are transferable.

The rescue app pairs to same-device wireless debugging (Android 11+) using pairing port/code and then connection port. Pair code is entered locally, never logged. Reuse a pinned existing ADB client, not a new protocol implementation. Pair credentials stay private to rescue and backup is disabled for rescue. No Shizuku dependency. Button explicitly stops the source app to obtain consistent files; it then reads with run-as over non-PTY binary streams. Preserve source DB+WAL while temporarily decoding SQLite in rescue-private cache, select configuration rows only, delete all raw artifacts on success/cancel/error/next startup. Never export notification content. Only source-data copies are opened by SQLite; the original is never opened for writing. Validate package/user/path arguments; never derive shell syntax from file contents.

## Portable file contract

One versioned UTF-8 JSON format shared by normal export and rescue conversion; source package/version/user/device metadata plus typed preference maps (boolean/int/long/float/double/string/string-set as applicable to storage) and explicit configuration row lists. Integers retain precision; no float conversion of longs. String-set ordering is deterministic. DataStore is decoded to typed values, not an opaque protobuf in the public file. Legacy SharedPreferences XML is decoded strictly, retaining known configuration with original types; unknown key names are listed in the preview, but their values are omitted because an unrecognized value may be a secret. The preview must warn that those settings were not transferred. Include schedule information in a readable versioned representation or existing validated JSON, with legacy migration through existing schedule logic; no silent default on a bad schedule. Current budget aggregates may be retained; spend detail/history excluded. Natural day/window reset must continue to apply.

Bound input sizes/counts before allocation, reject unknown format version, malformed/duplicate keys, invalid types/ranges, corrupt/truncated data, unexpected archive paths, and unsupported required settings before any destination mutation. Export/import preview names source and counts and reports omitted secrets/device grants. Reject source=destination in rescue. Full settings replace is explicit; preserve notification/history tables and unrelated current app internal state. Do not blindly copy all SharedPreferences into a fresh app.

Automation credential/receipt and recovery/ADB secrets never appear in portable files. After a successful import, the main-app startup adapter disables destination automation and removes its credential before normal initialization. This finalization is idempotent and retried while the Applied journal remains. A failed finalization blocks normal initialization. Rollback preserves destination automation. Re-enabling automation requires a new credential. No notification/usage text or app credentials in logs, errors or test fixtures. Backups are ordinary user-chosen documents and contain private configuration; no network upload. Use Storage Access Framework CreateDocument/OpenDocument, no broad storage permission.

## Import lifecycle and atomicity

Settings are distributed across SharedPreferences, DataStore, Room and in-memory caches. A sequence of setters while the listener runs is not an acceptable atomic import. Stage and fully validate a restore first. Require a visible apply-and-close/reopen flow; perform the actual restore before normal app initialization on next launch, while stores/workers/listener are quiescent. The preparation step must open/create the current Room schema before staging so startup restoration never creates a partial DB schema.

Use a durable import journal with previous and desired complete configuration. Capture previous settings at startup, so edits made after staging survive rollback. An interrupted Applying phase rolls back, even if all component writes had finished before the interruption. Every phase is idempotent across process death. On startup, apply all components before Hilt-created stores, WorkManager or user screens can read them. A store failure selects rollback durably, restores all previous components, and reports failure. If rollback itself fails, retain journal and block normal operation with recovery UI/retry; never present success or run with half-restored configuration. SQL writes touch only the explicit configuration tables in one transaction. Do not replace the Room database or historical tables. Offline DataStore replacement occurs only before its singleton exists; portable typed values must be prepared correctly with the public DataStore API. Receipt/journal live under no_backup and are excluded from export. Prefer a simpler design if it provides the same construction and tests.

## Pilot tests and evidence

Red tests must exercise production codec/converter and import coordinator ports: literal legacy XML + typed DataStore values/config rows -> exact portable values; lossless long/string-set behavior; explicit app/category/channel/schedule/budget settings preserved; histories/secrets excluded with positive controls; malformed/version/limit/type failures leave all stores unchanged; valid replace preserves history; failure on each store triggers rollback; crash/replay before/after phase boundaries converges without partial visible state; failures preserve recoverability and never acknowledge success. Test actual production seam, not a second algorithm. WHY/CLAIM/catches on each distinct case. Focused, bounded tests only; JVM tests where possible.

Runtime checks: old debuggable synthetic app data -> helper -> portable JSON -> new signed app -> matching configuration, with original source intact. Private owner data is not required in test logs or repo. Actual owner recovery requires owner pairing input/device interaction; no assumption that it already ran. The rescue APK should first be used to secure a backup before any signing-key uninstall/reinstall.

Defaults: settings only per owner; full explicit replace; personal user 0; secrets excluded; typed JSON with deterministic compact encoding; import requires cold start for consistency. This is a pilot, durability bar 9, correctness/security/architecture/legibility 6 pending stronger owner preferences. Physical wireless pairing and UI proof are separate from compile/JVM proof. # Settings recovery feasibility

The owner confirmed the prior installation should be debuggable and wants settings only, excluding notification and usage history. Recovery must read the prior package before any signature-change uninstall. ADB pairing itself does not grant arbitrary app-private-file access: AOSP run-as rejects packages not marked debuggable ([implementation](https://android.googlesource.com/platform/system/core/+/master/run-as/run-as.cpp)). The helper must probe this and report the actual result, not assume success.

The separate rescue app can use Android 11+ same-device wireless pairing, then a raw non-PTY ADB exec stream for run-as reads. Host/port and six-digit pairing code are entered locally in the helper. Pairing and normal connection use different ports; official workstation setup documents the distinction ([Android ADB guide](https://developer.android.com/tools/adb)). No phone recovery or pairing has occurred in this session.

Candidate client: pinned libadb-android 3.1.1, dual Apache-2.0/GPL-3.0-or-later with transitive LGPL notice. Its API supports pair, connect and openStream with arbitrary ADB service destinations ([tagged README](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MuntashirAkon/libadb-android/3.1.1/README.md)). Include license notices in rescue. Its SslUtils explicitly prefers the bundled org.conscrypt provider when present ([source](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MuntashirAkon/libadb-android/3.1.1/libadb/src/main/java/io/github/muntashirakon/adb/SslUtils.java)); therefore prefer the documented custom Conscrypt dependency rather than device hidden-API exemptions. Same-device pairing remains a device test, not a verified claim.

The upstream pairing implementation opens a Socket and performs blocking TLS/readFully without a socket timeout, and its manager holds a lock while pairing ([pairing source](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MuntashirAkon/libadb-android/3.1.1/libadb/src/main/java/io/github/muntashirakon/adb/PairingConnectionCtx.java), [manager source](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MuntashirAkon/libadb-android/3.1.1/libadb/src/main/java/io/github/muntashirakon/adb/AbsAdbConnectionManager.java)). Coroutine timeout alone cannot promise to cancel that I/O. Keep rescue jobs bounded with a real cancellation mechanism, e.g. isolate the bridge in a private worker process that can be stopped, or choose a client version providing explicit socket ownership/timeouts. Do not invent a new ADB protocol to solve it. The helper only needs loopback, not arbitrary remote hosts.

Local build constraints: nixed is ARM and currently has about 1.2 GiB available with 3 GiB swap occupied. Its checkout flake and nixpkgs aapt package support Linux x86_64, not Linux ARM. No adb/JDK/Gradle binary is on PATH. sonic SSH timed out. Boat is below the reserve; the prior ten-minute exception is exhausted. Prepare a JVM-only test runner through qex where feasible; Android APK builds still require a viable x86 build route or a fresh bounded owner exception. Never report unrun tests or unpaired recovery as complete.

## Answers to the parent's check-in questions

1. **Long.MAX_VALUE and typed DataStore without Android JSON.** The file format is typed by group, not by guessing: `longs` holds exact integer digits, `ints` holds 32-bit integers, `floats` and `doubles` hold decimals. The codec is production code in a plain JVM module and uses Jackson core streaming (`STRICT_DUPLICATE_DETECTION`, `StreamReadConstraints`), which behaves the same on the JVM and on Android. It reads a long token as a long and never as a double. DataStore reaches the converter as `Map<String, SettingValue>`, already decoded through the public DataStore API by an Android adapter. No protobuf bytes appear in the file. Tests pin `Long.MAX_VALUE`, `Long.MIN_VALUE` and `9007199254740993` (2^53 + 1, which a double cannot hold) against literal JSON.
2. **Excluding internals while keeping real settings.** One fixture is a literal `shared_pref.xml` that mixes both: `should_combine_db`, `today_usage_key`, `yesterday_usage_key`, onboarding flags, the automation credential/enabled/receipt keys and the budget spend ledger sit next to theme, app, category, channel, schedule and window settings. The test asserts the exact omitted key names and the exact kept map. It also encodes the result and asserts that sentinel strings planted in the excluded values (a fake credential, a fake notification title in the ledger, a value of an unknown key) are absent from the file bytes, while a sentinel from a kept setting is present. That presence check is the positive control. Unknown keys are listed by name in `unsupportedKeys`; their values are dropped.
3. **Journal phase that survives a failed rollback.** `RollingBack(previous, failure)`. It is written durably before the first restore and is only replaced by `RolledBack` after every component restored. If any restore throws, `startup()` returns `RecoveryRequired`, the journal still reads `RollingBack`, `blocksNormalOperation()` is true and `acknowledge()` throws. The test tells a safe block from a false success by asserting all four together, then heals the fault, calls `startup()` again and expects `RolledBack` with every store equal to the pre-import literal.

## What I built

New JVM module `:settings_portability` (package `ly.com.tahaben.settings_portability`). Both the rescue APK and the app depend on it. It has no Android SDK dependency.

| File | Content |
|---|---|
| `SettingValue.kt` | Sealed typed value: Bool, Int32, Int64, Float32, Float64, Text, TextSet. Real data classes. |
| `PortableSettings.kt` | Model, error codes, result types. Real data classes. |
| `SettingsCatalog.kt` | Which key is a setting, excluded, or unknown. **Stub.** |
| `PortableSettingsCodec.kt` | Versioned JSON encode/decode with limits. **Stub.** |
| `LegacySettingsConverter.kt` | Old files to portable settings, plus the `SemanticValidator` port. **Stub.** |
| `SettingsStores.kt` | Store ports, SQL ports, `SqlConfigurationRowsStore`. **Stub** for the SQL class. |
| `ImportJournal.kt` | Phase types, journal port. Real data types. |
| `ImportCoordinator.kt` | stage / startup / blocksNormalOperation / acknowledge, and `SettingsExporter`. **Stubs.** |

All stubs are `TODO(...)`, so every test that reaches one fails with `NotImplementedError`. The data classes carry no behavior.

The module applies `org.jetbrains.kotlin.jvm` without a version, relying on the Kotlin plugin already on the root classpath; this is unverified. I did not add the module to `app` or the rescue app. Nothing else changed. Existing tests are untouched.

## Design choices and the simpler options I took

- **Typed groups, compact canonical JSON.** The encoder emits compact JSON with fixed member order and sorted keys, so tests compare exact text. The spec says "readable"; a person can pretty-print it. Pretty output would make the golden depend on whitespace.
- **Catalog check lives outside the codec.** The codec checks structure (types, ranges, duplicates, limits). The catalog check (known key, right type, not excluded) happens in `stage`, `convert` and `export`. This lets the codec golden use float and double keys that no real key uses.
- **Unknown keys are names only.** The spec allowed "inert recovery data"; the parent's note asks for no blind passthrough. I carry names, not values.
- **Schedules stay verbatim.** The snapshot JSON (`notification_schedule_snapshot_v1`), the legacy `notification_delivery_schedule` string and the budget ints are copied unchanged. The destination app already upgrades legacy data on first read (`ScheduleCodec`, `DaySchedule.repairLegacy`), including the 23:59 repair. Re-implementing that in the converter would be a second algorithm. A `SemanticValidator` port rejects an undecodable schedule at convert and stage time instead of letting the app fall back to a default. The Android adapter for it is a missing seam.
- **Domain filtering in shared code.** `PreferencesStore` has `readAll()` and `apply(removeKeys, put)`. The coordinator computes the removal set from the catalog, so adapters cannot get the domain rule wrong and the "unrelated keys survive" claim is tested on the JVM.
- **Previous configuration is captured at startup, not at staging.** Settings may change between staging and restart; rolling back to the staging-time snapshot would lose those edits.
- **Interrupted apply rolls back instead of rolling forward.** Replaying `Applying` after a crash always restores the previous configuration and reports `INTERRUPTED`. It cannot loop on a crash that repeats, and it needs no attempt counter. The cost: a crash after every store was written still reverts the import, and the owner retries.
- **Terminal outcomes stay until acknowledged.** `Applied` and `RolledBack` remain in the journal until `acknowledge()`. A crash after the work still shows the outcome. Reporting is at-least-once; I did not promise exactly-once.
- **A real SQLite engine for the SQL claim.** A recording fake would only mirror the SQL text. The test uses `sqlite-jdbc` with `CREATE TABLE` statements copied from `app/schemas/.../7.json`, seeds history rows and checks they survive. # Settings portability: spec review, round 1

Reviewer: Opus, review only. Scope: spec, checklist, feasibility, red report, current `settings_portability` source and the 18 red tests (not compiled yet), plus the app manifest, `FarhanApplication`, `AppModule`, the Hilt entry points and the widget code. Nothing was built or run. Bar: durability 9, the rest 6.

Findings are ranked by how much configuration they could lose or corrupt.

## Answers to the two questions

### 1. Is the journaled rollback across three stores justified?

Yes, keep it. Without a journal, a crash between the Room commit and the DataStore or SharedPreferences commit leaves the app running with some old and some new settings, and the app cannot tell. The journal costs five durable writes and one sealed type. The red suite already pins its phases. The simpler alternatives are worse:
- Applying all three stores in one transaction is impossible across SharedPreferences, DataStore and SQLite.
- Rolling forward without a previous copy cannot recover when one store keeps failing.
- Replacing whole files (copying `shared_pref.xml` over the old one) would destroy the credential, the counters and the history tables that must survive.

Two parts are not justified. Cut them (F3, F5):
- A separate automation-finalization phase after `Applied`.
- A second, offline DataStore instance used only for the restore.

### 2. Which code paths could run on partly restored settings, and what is the smallest enforcement?

Android creates the `Application` before any service, receiver or activity in that process, apart from ContentProviders. So **for the normal path**, it is enough to run `startup()` synchronously in `FarhanApplication.onCreate()` **before `super.onCreate()`**. `Hilt_FarhanApplication.onCreate` performs the injection that builds `Configuration`, `DefaultWorkerFactory` and the store singletons. None of that exists yet at that point. The only ContentProvider is `androidx.startup.InitializationProvider` (with `WorkManagerInitializer` removed), and it reads no Farhan settings.

The open case is `RecoveryRequired` (rollback failed, or the journal is unreadable). Skipping `super.onCreate()` does not help, because every `@AndroidEntryPoint` builds the singleton component on its own when it injects. Two concrete paths would still run on mixed settings:

1. **`NotificationService` (`NotificationListenerService`, `@AndroidEntryPoint`).** The system binds it as soon as the process exists, and listener binding is often what starts the process. Injection pulls the SharedPreferences, DataStore and Room singletons. `onNotificationPosted` then filters with a mixed priority, schedule and budget, and it **writes** budget spend, the ledger and the queue.
2. **`ScheduleAutomationReceiver` (exported, `@AndroidEntryPoint`) and `NotificationDeliveryReceiver` (BOOT_COMPLETED and exact alarm).** The first writes schedule settings when an external intent arrives. The second delivers or holds queued notifications using a mixed schedule. `AccessibilityService`, `TimeLimitService`, `WidgetBroadcast` and `LauncherActivity` (a HOME activity, which runs constantly when Farhan is the default launcher) also read mixed settings.

Smallest enforcement that leaves the recovery screen working (about 60 lines, no new state file):

- Add a manifest activity `ImportRecoveryActivity`: a plain `ComponentActivity`, **not** Hilt, `android:enabled="false"`, with its own MAIN/LAUNCHER filter. It builds its stores without Hilt, calls `startup()` on the Retry button, and shows the failure reason.
- In `FarhanApplication.onCreate`, before `super.onCreate()`:
  - If the journal blocks normal operation: enable the recovery activity first. Then disable every other component of the package, listed at runtime through `PackageManager.getPackageInfo(GET_ACTIVITIES|GET_SERVICES|GET_RECEIVERS)` (no hand-written list), using `DONT_KILL_APP`. Then kill the process. This also stops the component whose bind started the process. Return without calling `super.onCreate()`, so no Hilt, WorkManager or ACRA starts.
  - If it does not block: put every component back to `COMPONENT_ENABLED_STATE_DEFAULT` (which keeps the manifest's own `enabled` values), then disable the recovery activity **last**.
- The recovery activity being enabled is the only marker, so a crash at any step converges on the next start. The app never toggles components today (grep for `setComponentEnabledSetting`: no hits), so restoring DEFAULT cannot undo a user choice.
- WorkManager stays uninitialized in a blocked process. `SystemJobService` logs and ignores jobs when WorkManager is not initialized. A device check should confirm this.

Why not the alternatives:
- **Throwing in `Application` or in the `AppModule` providers.** The launcher crashes, so the user has no way to reach the recovery screen, and the listener crash-loops.
- **A gate check in each entry point.** That is ten places, Hilt injects before most of the component code runs, and any new component added later is missed.

Seam tests for this (instrumented or Robolectric, not pure JVM):
- **Blocked:** a RollingBack journal plus a bind to `NotificationService` leaves the stores byte-identical and leaves only the recovery activity enabled.
- **Healed:** after Retry succeeds, all components are back at DEFAULT and the recovery activity is disabled.
- **Crash between toggles:** a crash at any point converges on the next start.
- **Normal path:** with a Staged journal, the first `NotificationService` injection sees the desired settings (startup ran before injection).

## Findings

**F1. A red test is wrong for a correct implementation (crash sweep, rollback variant).** `ImportCoordinatorTest.crashSweep` with `failApplyOfShared` at crash point 1: the process dies while writing the Applying journal, so the journal is still `Staged`. The `is Staged` branch then expects `Applied(expectedPreview)` and the desired stores. But the injected failure is still active, so a correct replay rolls back to `RolledBack(STORE_FAILED, SHARED_PREFERENCES)`, and the test fails. Green would have to break the coordinator or edit the test silently. Fix before green: pass the expected terminal result into `crashSweep` as a literal (`Applied` for the plain sweeps, `RolledBack(STORE_FAILED, SHARED_PREFERENCES)` plus the previous stores for the rollback sweeps).

**F2. A wrong implementation that passes: the journal-first claim is not pinned by the plain sweeps.** Take an implementation that skips the `Applying` record, keeps `previous` in memory, writes the stores straight from `Staged`, and rolls back from memory on an exception. It passes the store-failure test and both plain sweeps, because replaying `Staged` simply re-applies. Only the corrected rollback sweep (F1) would catch it, and only because a crash in the in-memory rollback leaves `Staged` with stores in the desired state. Add an explicit case: crash after the first store write; the journal must read `Applying`, and replay must give `RolledBack(INTERRUPTED)` with the previous stores. Mutation 3 in the red report assumes this case exists.

**F3. Fold automation revocation into the apply instead of a finalization phase after it.** The accepted design (the adapter disables automation after `Applied`, retries while Applied remains, and a failure blocks startup) needs things the coordinator cannot express:
- `StartupResult.Applied.allowsNormalOperation` is hard-coded `true`, so the "finalization failed" state has no type. The adapter has to invent a second blocking path, separate from `RecoveryRequired`, with its own recovery UI.
- `stage()` over an unacknowledged `Applied` journal (allowed by "replaces an older Staged", untested) would erase the obligation to revoke.

Simpler, and equivalent for the owner:
- Treat the three automation keys as **import-managed** in the catalog.
- On apply, the desired SharedPreferences commit removes the credential and the receipt keys and puts `enabled=false`. This happens in the same atomic commit, so revocation succeeds or fails with the import.
- `previous` captures those keys too (the journal lives under `no_backup`, in the same private storage as the credential), so rollback restores destination automation untouched.

This removes one phase, one retry loop and one blocking state. Test change: `expectedSharedAfterImport` loses the credential and gains `enabled=false`, and the rollback cases keep it. If the parent keeps the adapter design, then at least make `Applied` carry `pendingFinalization` and make `acknowledge()` refuse until finalization is done, with a test.

**F4. Widget configuration is not modelled (red verifier's finding: agreed, the gap is real).** Glance keeps per-widget state in `files/datastore/appWidget-<id>.preferences_pb` (Glance `PreferencesGlanceStateDefinition`). The user keys there are `widget_theme_colors`, `widget_ui_mode`, `widget_style`, `widget_compare_yesterday` and `text_size`. Exclude `today_time_today`, `yesterday_time_today` and `is_loading` as derived values. The refresh interval (`UsageWidgetConfigActivity:177`) lives only in WorkManager's unique periodic request and is never read back, so it is device state: name it in the preview and do not transfer it. Smallest model:
- Add `widgetProfiles: List<WidgetProfile>` to `SettingsConfiguration`, holding the five typed fields only. **No widget id.** The list is deduplicated and sorted in a fixed order.
- **Restore** writes the profiles as one catalog key in the main DataStore (`imported_widget_profiles_v1`, a validated JSON string). That puts them inside the same journaled apply, with no Glance DataStore writes at startup and no mapping of widget ids. `WidgetConfigActivity.getWidgetConfiguration` uses the first imported profile as the starting selection when the widget's own state is empty. When there are two or more, it shows them as presets.
- The **preview** says: "N widget styles found. Add the widgets to your home screen again; their saved styles appear as choices."
- **Rescue** lists `files/datastore` through `run-as`. It accepts only names matching `^appWidget-[0-9]{1,10}\.preferences_pb$`, and no other names are passed to the shell.
- **Normal export** reads `GlanceAppWidgetManager.getGlanceIds` plus `getAppWidgetState` and carries the imported profiles that are not yet in use.
- Tests: a literal per-id map becomes the exact profile, with derived keys absent (positive control: `text_size` is present); two identical widgets produce one profile; an invalid enum name gives `SEMANTIC_REJECTED`.

**F5. Use one DataStore instance for both restore and Hilt, not an offline replacement.** DataStore 1.1.3 refuses a second active instance for the same file in one process. The offline restore instance would need its own scope, cancelled and joined before Hilt runs, and that only shows up on a device. Simpler: a small non-Hilt `ProcessStores` holder creates the `shared_pref` SharedPreferences, the `farhan_data_store` DataStore and the Room database once. `startup()` uses the holder before `super.onCreate()`, and the three `AppModule` `@Provides` return the same instances. SharedPreferences is already cached per process, and Room needs the same treatment for its invalidation tracker. That drops the spec sentence "only before its singleton exists". Note: Room's `assertNotMainThread` blocks DAO and transaction APIs on the main thread. Run the apply on a worker thread and `join()` it, or use `openHelper.writableDatabase` directly.

**F6. The 10,000-character string bound can make the app's own exports impossible to import. The 11-character fixture is wrong.**
- **Fixture.** The test fixture's own envelope holds `ly.com.tahaben.farhan_alpha` (27 characters), `farhan-settings` (15) and `sharedPreferences` (17). A global bound of 11 must reject that fixture, yet the test expects it to be accepted. Fix: use a value longer than every envelope token, for example `"x".repeat(40)`, accepted at `maxStringLength = 40` and rejected at 39. Do not use the longest required token (27) as the boundary: then a failure would not show which token tripped it. Count member names as well as values, so the bound really is global.
- **Jackson.** I believe `StreamReadConstraints.maxStringLength` is only checked when Jackson's text buffer grows, so it will not catch a 40/39 boundary. The codec should check the length of each token itself. Verify this on the first run.
- **Real sizes.** `notification_app_queue_v1` is a single JSON string (DefaultPreferences:305) of about 80 characters per configured app, so roughly 125 apps exceed 10,000. The schedule snapshot and delivery-settings JSON grow the same way. The parent's preferred global bound is fine; the default number is not derived from real data. Set it to 262,144 (still under `maxBytes`, which already caps memory), or measure the largest real value and document the margin.
- **Exporter.** Add an encode-side guard: `SettingsExporter` decodes its own bytes with the default limits and fails loudly before it writes the SAF document. The two path-level tests in the encoder, the exporter and the round-trip suite have no oversize case. Add one with a 12,000-character queue string.

**F7. The rescue must read `shared_pref.xml.bak` when it exists.** `SharedPreferencesImpl` renames the file to `.bak` before rewriting it, and on load uses the `.bak` file whenever it is present. If the old app was killed mid-commit (or by a force-stop during a write), `shared_pref.xml` can be truncated while `.bak` holds the real settings. Copy both and choose exactly as Android does. Add a converter or rescue test: a truncated main file plus a valid `.bak` gives the `.bak` content.

For DataStore, read only the main `.preferences_pb` and ignore the `.tmp` file. Keep the `.preferences_pb` extension on the copy, because `PreferenceDataStoreFactory` rejects any other extension.

For SQLite, copy `apps_db` together with whichever of `-wal` and `-journal` exists. Low-RAM devices use TRUNCATE journal mode, not WAL. Open only the copy, read-write (a WAL database cannot be opened read-only without `-shm`). Check that the source file sizes and modification times are the same before and after the copy.

**F8. Untested coordinator states.**
- Stage while the journal is `Applying`/`RollingBack` must return `NotStaged(IMPORT_IN_PROGRESS)` with zero operations.
- Stage while `Applied`/`RolledBack` is unacknowledged: decide (default: refuse until acknowledged, so the outcome is never lost).

`previous` must capture the raw values of every catalog-domain key **without type validation**. If an older build stored a catalog key with another type, a validating capture drops it, and rollback then deletes a setting the user had. Add a test: a previous store holding `notification_flood_threshold` as `Int64`, then a failed apply, must restore it as `Int64`.

**F9. Rescue worker process: agreed, with two conditions.**
- Kill only the `:adb_bridge` process, with `Process.killProcess(pid)` from the same uid.
- Accept only loopback hosts (`127.0.0.1` or `::1`) and ports 1–65535.
- Keep the rescue's ADB key in its private storage and delete it after success. Afterwards, tell the owner to remove the rescue from the paired devices list and turn wireless debugging off. Otherwise an authorized ADB key stays on the phone. One line in the cleanup step covers this.

Validate in the bridge process, not only in the UI:
- **Package.** The source package matches `^[a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9_]*(\.[a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9_]*)+$` and is not the rescue's own package.
- **Debuggable.** Probe with `run-as <pkg> id`. "Package not debuggable" maps to a specific error ("this build can't be read; it was not built debuggable"), never a generic failure.
- **Binary reads.** Read with `exec:run-as <pkg> cat <fixed relative path>` over the raw `exec:` service. `shell:` would add a PTY and convert line endings.

**F10. After a force-stop, the old app's queued notifications stay held.** A force-stop cancels its exact alarms, and a stopped app does not receive BOOT_COMPLETED. Notifications the old Farhan was holding are not delivered until the old app is opened again, and they are lost if it is uninstalled. They are history, so they are rightly excluded. The rescue's final screen should still say: "Open the old Farhan once if it was holding notifications, before you uninstall it."

## What to change before green

1. Fix the crash-sweep expectation (F1) and add the journal-first crash case (F2).
2. Correct the string-limit fixture and decide the default from real data (F6). Add the exporter oversize test.
3. Decide F3 (fold revocation into the apply, recommended) and update `expectedSharedAfterImport`.
4. Add `widgetProfiles` to the model and the red tests (F4).
5. Add the F8 coordinator cases.

These can follow in the Android-adapter red batch: F5, F7 and F9 tests, and the startup-gate tests from question 2.

Hollow tests: none found among the coordinator assertions apart from F1/F2. Each loop has a membership pin and each absence check has a control. The exporter test passes `SemanticValidator { null }`, so it does not show that the exporter calls the validator at all. That is low priority, but the claim "export never writes a file stage would reject" needs either a validator that rejects or the self-decode guard from F6.

I've written the round-1 review to `/home/mini/Documents/repos/Farhan/research/settings-portability-spec-review.md`. Nothing was built or run, and the claims about Android and library behaviour come from reading code and docs, not from a device.

**Your two questions**

1. **Is the three-store journaled rollback worth it?** Yes. The cheaper options either can't recover when one store keeps failing, or would wipe the credential, counters and history tables. Two pieces aren't worth it and should go (F3 and F5 below).
2. **What can still run on half-restored settings, and how do we stop it without locking out the recovery screen?**
   - **Normal path:** call `startup()` synchronously in `FarhanApplication.onCreate()` *before* `super.onCreate()`. That runs before Hilt injection, WorkManager and ACRA, and Android creates the Application before any other component in the process (ContentProviders aside). The only provider is androidx.startup with the WorkManager initializer removed.
   - **The two paths that still run if recovery fails:** `NotificationService`, which the system binds on process start; it injects the stores, filters with a mixed schedule and budget, and writes spend, ledger and queue. And the receivers: the exported `ScheduleAutomationReceiver`, which writes the schedule, plus `NotificationDeliveryReceiver` on boot or alarm. Skipping `super.onCreate()` doesn't stop them, because each Hilt component builds its own dependencies when it injects.
   - **Smallest fix:** add a recovery screen that doesn't use Hilt, disabled in the manifest, with its own launcher icon. When the journal is blocked, enable that screen first, disable every other component (listed at runtime from PackageManager, so a new component can't be missed), then kill the process. When it unblocks, put the components back to their defaults and disable the recovery screen last. Whether that screen is enabled is the only marker needed, so a crash at any step sorts itself out on the next start. The app never toggles components today, so restoring defaults can't undo a user choice.

**Findings that should change things before green**
- **F1:** a red test fails a correct implementation. In the rollback crash sweep, at crash point 1 the journal is still `Staged`, the injected failure is still active, and the replay correctly ends at `RolledBack(STORE_FAILED)`. The test expects `Applied`.
- **F2:** a short wrong implementation passes the plain crash sweeps. It skips the `Applying` record, keeps the previous settings in memory and rolls back from there. A crash-after-first-store-write case is needed.
- **F3:** I'm pushing back on the accepted automation-revocation adapter. `StartupResult.Applied` always allows normal operation, so "revocation failed" has no state to live in. And staging over an unacknowledged `Applied` journal would erase the revocation it still owes. Simpler: remove the credential and set enabled=false inside the same atomic SharedPreferences commit, and capture those keys in the previous snapshot so rollback keeps the destination's automation.
- **F4 (widgets):** I agree with the verifier.
  - Add `widgetProfiles` to the configuration model: the five typed fields, no widget id, deduplicated and in a fixed order.
  - On import, store them as one validated key in the main DataStore. That keeps them inside the same journaled apply.
  - The widget config screen then offers them as starting choices, and the preview tells the owner to add the widgets again.
  - Exclude the derived keys. The refresh interval only lives in WorkManager, so it's device state and not transferred.
  - The rescue helper must accept only file names matching `appWidget-<digits>.preferences_pb`.
- **F6 (string limit):** fix the fixture. The test document's own header already contains a 27-character string, so a global limit of 11 must reject it. Use a 40-character value, accepted at 40 and rejected at 39.
  - I believe Jackson's own string limit is only checked when its buffer grows, so the codec should check lengths itself.
  - **The bigger risk:** a default of 10,000 means the app can produce exports it can't import. The app queue is one JSON string of about 80 characters per app, so roughly 125 apps go over. Raise the default to 262,144 (or measure real data), and have export decode its own output before writing the file.
- **F8:** add tests for staging during an in-progress or unacknowledged import. Also capture previous values without type checks; otherwise a rollback deletes a setting an older build stored with a different type.

**For the Android adapter work, not before green**
- **F5:** use one shared set of store instances for both the startup restore and Hilt. DataStore 1.1.3 refuses a second instance on the same file.
- **F7:** the rescue must use `shared_pref.xml.bak` when it exists. Android writes that backup before rewriting the file, and after a mid-write kill only the backup is intact. Copy the database with whichever of `-wal` or `-journal` exists.
- **F9:** keep the separate worker process for the ADB bridge, but accept loopback hosts only and validate in that process. The rescue's ADB key needs cleaning up, and the owner should remove the pairing and turn wireless debugging off afterwards.
- **F10:** a force-stop leaves the old app's held notifications undelivered. The rescue's last screen should tell the owner to open the old app once before uninstalling it.

These three are my unverified claims; check them on the first compile or device run:
- Jackson only checks string length when its buffer grows.
- DataStore 1.1.3 refuses a second instance on the same file.
- WorkManager's job service skips jobs quietly when WorkManager isn't initialized.

I'd most like to argue F3 and the default string limit with you before the review closes.
